lessons.title: 1929: The Great Crash and the Great Depression

body.text: 1929 was not one bad day. It was a crash, a convincing recovery that fooled everyone, and then a three year collapse, made far worse by leverage and by policy mistakes.

children.text: The Great Crash is the reference point for every crash that came after it. Whenever the Nifty falls sharply, someone asks whether this is "another 1929". To answer that sensibly, you need to know what actually happened: how the boom was built, what broke in October 1929, why the worst losses came years later, and why a stock market crash turned into the Great Depression. As you read, match each phase to the five bubble stages from Chapter 1.
The Roaring Twenties: Displacement and Boom

The 1920s gave America a genuine displacement. Electricity reached ordinary homes, cars rolled off assembly lines, radio created a mass market, and company profits rose. Shares in the new industries became the talk of the country, from bankers to shoeshine boys. Between August 1921 and September 1929, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about six times.

stats.label: Dow, August 1921
stats.context: The low before the boom began

stats.label: Brokers' Loans, Summer 1929
stats.context: More than all the currency in circulation in the US

markDefs.definition: Buying shares with a small cash deposit and borrowing the rest from a broker, with the shares held as collateral.
Loans made by brokers to customers buying shares on margin, typically funded by bank borrowing. Their total is a direct measure of leverage in the stock market.

children.text: What turned a boom into a bubble was borrowed money. Investors could buy shares
on margin
by putting down as little as 10% of the price and borrowing the rest. Brokers funded these loans by borrowing from banks. By the summer of 1929,
brokers' loans
had swollen to about $8.5 billion. In the language of Lesson 1.3, the entire market was running at leverage that would make a modern MTF desk nervous.

body.title: Your Turn: The 1929 Margin Buyer
body.prompt: In 1929, an investor buys $1,000 of shares by paying $100 in cash and borrowing $900 from his broker. By what percentage does the share price need to fall to wipe out his entire $100?
body.explanation: He is at 10x leverage. A 10% fall takes the shares from $1,000 to $900, exactly the size of the loan, leaving him with nothing. On Black Monday and Black Tuesday alone, the Dow fell about 23% in two sessions. A 10% margin buyer who did not add cash was wiped out more than twice over, and his broker sold his shares into a falling market to recover the loan.

body.text: Compare this with India today. Brokers' MTF desks lend at most up to 80% of a trade on eligible stocks, and SEBI's peak margin rules limit intraday leverage to about 5x. In 1929, 10x leverage was ordinary and unregulated. Many of the modern rules you trade under exist because of what happened next.

children.text: October 1929: The Week Everything Broke

The market began wobbling after its September peak. On 15 October, Irving Fisher, one of America's most respected economists, told an audience that stock prices had reached "what looks like a permanently high plateau". Nine days later, the selling began in earnest.

events.title: The Peak
events.description: The Dow closes at 381.17, the top of an eight year bull market.

events.title: The Plateau Speech
events.description: Irving Fisher declares that stock prices look permanently high. It becomes one of the most quoted forecasting errors in market history.

events.title: Black Thursday
events.description: Panic selling hits at the open, and a record 12.9 million shares change hands. Leading bankers pool their money, and NYSE vice president Richard Whitney makes a show of bidding 205 for 10,000 shares of US Steel. The market steadies by the close.

events.title: Black Monday
events.description: The bankers do not return. The Dow falls 12.8% to close at 260.64 as margin calls force selling.

events.title: Black Tuesday
events.description: A record 16.4 million shares trade and the Dow falls another 11.7% to 230.07. Ticker machines run hours behind, so investors do not even know what their shares are worth.

events.title: The First Bottom
events.description: The Dow closes at 198.69, 47.9% below its September peak, in just over two months.

body.title: Why the Rescue Failed
body.question: On Black Thursday, the bankers' pool steadied the market by buying shares. Four days later, the market fell nearly 13% anyway. Using what you learned in Chapter 1, what is the best explanation?
options: The bankers ran out of money on the first day
Buying shares cannot stop forced sellers: margin calls triggered by the earlier falls kept pushing shares onto the market regardless of price
The US government ordered the bankers to stop buying
Investors realised that company profits had fallen 13% over the weekend
body.explanation: The pool could calm nerves for a day, but it could not change the arithmetic of leverage. Thousands of margin accounts were already below required levels. Over the weekend, brokers issued margin calls, and on Monday the positions of everyone who could not pay were sold at any price. That forced supply overwhelmed the buying support, and the bankers chose not to throw more money at it. This is the selling spiral from Lesson 1.3 on a national scale.

children.text: The Recovery That Fooled Everyone

markDefs.definition: A sharp but temporary rise in prices during a longer downtrend. It convinces many investors the decline is over before the fall resumes.

children.text: Here is the part of 1929 most people never hear about. After the November low, the market bounced hard. By April 1930 the Dow had risen nearly half from its bottom. Business leaders declared the worst was over, and many investors who had sat out the crash bought back in. It was a classic
bear market rally

body.label: The Cost of Buying the First Dip
body.context: An investor who bought at the November 1929 low of 198.69, thinking the crash was over, watched the Dow fall to 41.22 by July 1932. The Dow did not close above its 1929 peak again until November 1954.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The Dow's 48% rise from November 1929 to April 1930, followed by a collapse to new lows, is an example of a bear market ___.
body.explanation: A bear market rally is a sharp, temporary rise inside a longer decline. They are dangerous precisely because they are convincing: a 48% rise feels like a new bull market. The lesson is not that every rise after a crash is a trap, since the Nifty's 2020 recovery was real. The lesson is that a rise alone does not tell you the damage underneath has healed.

children.text: From Market Crash to Great Depression

markDefs.definition: A sustained fall in the general price level. It raises the real burden of debt, because borrowers repay loans with money that is worth more than when they borrowed it.

children.text: A stock market crash does not automatically cause a depression. What turned 1929 into a decade of misery was what happened in the real economy and, above all, how policymakers responded. Banks that had lent into the boom began to fail, and panicked depositors ran to withdraw cash, bringing down more banks. The Federal Reserve failed to stop the money supply from shrinking. Prices fell, a
deflation
that made every loan harder to repay. In 1930, the Smoot-Hawley Tariff raised US import duties, and other countries retaliated, shrinking world trade.

children.text: How the Depression Reached India

India in 1929 was a British colony whose economy rested on agriculture, and the Depression arrived through crop prices rather than share prices. As world demand collapsed, prices of wheat, jute, cotton and rice crashed. Farmers' incomes fell, but the land revenue they owed the colonial government did not, pushing rural households deeper into debt. Colonial policy kept the rupee linked to sterling rather than letting it adjust, which tightened credit further.

cells: Fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, a drop of about 37%
Fell by about half between 1928 and 1934
Indians sold household gold to survive, and net gold exports reached about 7.7 million ounces, worth ₹57.98 crore, in 1931 to 1932
Largely unchanged, so the real burden on farmers rose sharply as prices fell

body.text: The agrarian distress of the early 1930s fed directly into Indian politics. Rural anger over prices, debt and revenue gave strength to the Civil Disobedience Movement launched in 1930. A crash that began on Wall Street reshaped lives in Punjab and Bengal, a pattern of global contagion you will see again in 2008.

children.text: What 1929 Changed Forever
The Great Crash produced the modern architecture of market regulation, and India's own system follows the same ideas.

body.caption: Reforms Born From 1929, and Their Indian Parallels

cells: Required companies selling shares to the public to disclose material information
SEBI's disclosure rules for IPOs, including the offer document every issuer must file
Created the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to regulate markets and brokers
SEBI, set up in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992
Federal margin requirements, under the 1934 Act
Gave the Federal Reserve power to limit how much investors could borrow to buy shares
SEBI and exchange margin rules, including peak margin and MTF norms
Created federal deposit insurance and separated commercial and investment banking
DICGC deposit insurance, covering up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank

body.title: The Ironic Fate of Richard Whitney

children.text: Richard Whitney, the man who stood on the NYSE floor on Black Thursday and bid for US Steel to calm the market, became a hero of the crash. He went on to serve as president of the New York Stock Exchange.

In 1938, Whitney was convicted of embezzlement, having misused money belonging to clients and others to cover his own failing investments. He was sent to Sing Sing prison. His downfall helped push reform of how the exchange governed itself.

The lesson for investors: the most visible, trusted figure in a market is not automatically a sound one. In India, the heroes of the 1992 and 2001 bull runs, whom you will meet in Chapter 4, followed a similar arc.

body.title: "It Can Never Happen Again"
body.scenario: At a family dinner, your uncle, who has invested in shares since the 1990s, says: "A 1929 style crash is impossible in India today. SEBI exists, there are circuit breakers, and RBI would never let the banks collapse. A 90% fall simply cannot happen."
body.prompt: Which parts of his argument are reasonable, and which parts go too far? Use what you learned in this lesson.
body.modelAnswer: Several parts are reasonable. The conditions that made 1929 so catastrophic have been deliberately addressed: leverage is regulated through margin rules, deposit insurance covers ordinary savers, disclosure rules exist, and central banks now respond to crises by adding liquidity rather than letting the money supply shrink, as RBI did in 2020. That makes a repeat of the full 1929 to 1932 collapse, driven by the same policy failures, much less likely. But the argument goes too far in three ways. First, circuit breakers pause trading; they do not stop prices falling over days and weeks, and in 2008 the Nifty still fell about 60%. Second, regulation cannot prevent bubbles in individual stocks or sectors, and many Indian stocks have fallen 80% or 90% or more even as the index recovered. Third, new forms of leverage keep appearing, such as heavy F&O trading and promoter pledging, which rules only partly contain. A fair conclusion: an index level repeat of 1929 is unlikely, but large crashes are not impossible, and individual portfolios can still suffer 1929 sized losses.

points: The 1920s boom rested on a real displacement, but 10% margin buying and $8.5 billion of brokers' loans turned it into a leveraged bubble
The crash hit hardest in October 1929: the Dow fell 12.8% on Black Monday and 11.7% on Black Tuesday, and was down 48% from its peak by mid November
The deepest losses came after a 48% bear market rally, as the Dow slid a further 86% to 41.22 by July 1932
Bank failures, a shrinking money supply, deflation and trade wars turned a market crash into the Great Depression
India felt the Depression through collapsing crop prices, rural debt and distress sales of gold
Disclosure rules, market regulators, margin limits and deposit insurance all trace back to 1929, and SEBI and DICGC play those roles in India today
